Consider the differential relevance of migration status, religion, Roma descent, and African descent across the EU member states; Farkas’s comparative review (Farkas, 2017) documents both the variation in collection practices and the definitional inconsistency across jurisdictions. These kinds of conceptual uncertainty can easily render a measurement effort foundationally unsound, no matter how much ingenuity goes into the technical measurement stack. After all, what is the value of a fairness measurement relative to a demographic attribute upon which both decision-makers and stakeholders have no mutually settled definition?

From the privacy engineering contributions, our HE adaptations catalog (Section 3) is also highly transferable for anyone aiming to develop a privatized analytic capability that relies on additive homomorphic encryption. Ratio estimation, fixed-point encoding, pre-encryption comparison, signed-number encoding, and bootstrap hypothesis testing apply to any ratio-form statistic computed under additive HE. These patterns are not specific to fairness metrics or to race/ethnicity measurement; they address general limitations of additive homomorphic encryption that arise in any applied setting.

From the composed protocol, the two-party architecture with PSI-based join and homomorphic aggregation provides a reusable template for secure measurement protocols. Governance controls (legal approval, minimum population thresholds, differencing-attack prevention) are separable from the cryptographic protocol and can be adapted to other institutional contexts.

8.5. Limitations

  1. (1)

    Geographical scope. BISG depends on U.S. Census surname and geolocation frequency tables. Extension to the EU or other jurisdictions requires similarly well-curated census data with well-defined demographic groupings. Recent explorations of EU equality data suggest these standards are difficult to replicate outside the U.S., which constrains the framework’s near-term international applicability.

  2. (2)

    BISG calibration. The BISG model is not fine-tuned for the target member population. Validation confirms it is informative-but-imperfect for our target population. Calibration shortfalls in the demographic estimation propagate to downstream measurements. The Self-ID comparison characterizes accuracy only for Self-ID respondents, who measurably and systematically differ from non-respondents.

  3. (3)

    Diffuse posteriors. For members whose surnames and locations are not strongly associated with any single group, BISG produces diffuse posteriors (e.g., near-uniform across categories). These members contribute nearly equally to every group’s statistic, diluting the measurement signal. If a test population has many such members, measured disparities will be attenuated toward zero.

  4. (4)

    Geofencing and population selection. Excluding non-USA members and certain state residents alters the test population. Fairness comparisons within the included population remain valid, but they may not generalize to the excluded population. Quantifying the impact of such exclusions on measurement representativeness is an important open problem.

  5. (5)

    LOT independence assumption. The probabilistic LOT estimator (Equation 8) replaces the joint group indicator 𝕀⁡(Ri=a∩Ri+1=b)\mathbb{I}({R_{i}=a}\cap{R_{i+1}=b}) with the product 𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=a)⋅𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri+1=b)\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=a)\cdot\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i+1}=b), assuming independence between adjacent candidates’ demographics. In practice, adjacent candidates in a ranked list may share characteristics because the ranking model clusters similar candidates. BISG posteriors depend on geolocation so spatial clustering can induce positive correlation between adjacent posteriors and possibly deflate the denominator for cross-group pairs. The direction of the resulting bias depends on the correlation structure; characterizing its magnitude for specific ranking systems is an open question.

8.6. Future Work

  1. (1)

    BISG refinement. The current BISG model uses generic U.S. Census frequency tables without adaptation to the target member population. Calibrating the model for this population would improve estimation accuracy. Methods include fine-tuning the prior using Self-ID data (with appropriate privacy protections) and incorporating additional demographic signals beyond surname and geolocation.

  2. (2)

    Uncertainty quantification. Current measurements report bootstrap confidence intervals for the final disparity statistics, but these intervals capture only sampling variability. They do not account for uncertainty in the BISG estimates themselves. Propagating BISG prediction uncertainty through the estimators would provide a more complete picture of measurement reliability, but this is technically challenging because it requires characterizing the joint distribution of BISG errors across the test population.

  3. (3)

    Cross-jurisdictional extension. Extending PPRE to non-U.S. jurisdictions depends on the availability of suitable demographic data. The EU’s fragmented equality data landscape presents particular challenges, and any extension must also navigate differing legal frameworks governing the use of demographic data for algorithmic fairness evaluation. The signal-processing pillar of PPRE is modular enough to accommodate alternative demographic models, but the practical barriers are substantial.

9. Conclusion

We presented PPRE: a production-deployed system for privacy-preserving race/ethnicity fairness measurement. PPRE monitors AI systems for equal treatment when demographic data is severely limited and privacy constraints are strict. The system rests on three pillars.

Demographic signal processing. BISG generates probabilistic race/ethnicity posteriors from surname and geolocation; sparse Self-ID records provide calibration. Probabilistic disparity estimators replace hard demographic indicators with soft ones, generalizing standard fairness metrics to operate on probability distributions. This gives weighted-average statistics that are both accurate and compatible with encrypted computation.

Privacy primitives and extensions. Commutative encryption enables private set intersection. Additive homomorphic encryption supports computation on ciphertexts. Local differential privacy protects Self-ID records at the input stage. A catalog of five HE adaptations extends the toolkit to support the division, comparison, and hypothesis testing that production fairness metrics require. These adaptations are general-purpose: they apply to any ratio-form statistic under additive HE, not only to fairness metrics or race/ethnicity measurement.

Protocol composition. A custom two-party computation protocol composes these elements so that neither party ever observes the other’s plaintext inputs, with all member-level data ephemeral throughout. Production fairness measurements of two AI ranking systems using LOT and MQOS-NDCG found no statistically significant race-related biases. All measurements ran entirely in ciphertext space with bootstrap significance testing.

PPRE serves as an existence proof that privatized multi-party fairness measurement is feasible at industrial scale. The implementation experience also reveals where the hard problems lie: testing and debugging multiparty flows incurs costs at least an order of magnitude higher than single-party equivalents. And geographically scoped demographic models introduce population-selection effects that must be carefully characterized. The design principles, protocol architecture, and engineering patterns documented here offer a concrete reference for institutions building similar infrastructure.

Appendix A Cryptographic and Statistical Primitives

This appendix provides complete formal definitions of the cryptographic and statistical primitives summarized in Section 2.

A.1. Commutative Encryption

A commutative encryption scheme 𝖢𝗈𝗆=(𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖣𝖾𝖼)\mathsf{Com}=(\mathsf{Com.KeyGen},\mathsf{Com.Enc},\mathsf{Com.Dec}) is a symmetric encryption scheme (with a deterministic encryption algorithm) over message space ℳ\mathcal{M}:

  • •

    𝗌𝗄←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)\mathsf{sk}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com.KeyGen}(1^{\lambda})

  • •

    𝖼𝗍←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗌𝗄​(m)\mathsf{ct}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com.Enc}_{\mathsf{sk}}(m)

  • •

    m/⊥←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄(𝖼𝗍)m/\bot\leftarrow\mathsf{Com.Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}(\mathsf{ct})

  • •

    For any two keys 𝗌𝗄1,𝗌𝗄2\mathsf{sk}_{1},\mathsf{sk}_{2} and any message m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M},

    𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗌𝗄1(𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗌𝗄2(m))=𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗌𝗄2(𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗌𝗄1(m))\mathsf{Com.Enc}_{\mathsf{sk}_{1}}(\mathsf{Com.Enc}_{\mathsf{sk}_{2}}(m))=\mathsf{Com.Enc}_{\mathsf{sk}_{2}}(\mathsf{Com.Enc}_{\mathsf{sk}_{1}}(m))

A popular instantiation is the Pohlig-Hellman cipher over an Elliptic Curve group 𝒢\mathcal{G} in which the Decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH) assumption holds. A random oracle 𝖱𝖮\mathsf{RO} maps arbitrary messages into 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Section 7 details our specific instantiation.

This commutativity property, combined with a fresh 𝖱𝖮\mathsf{RO} instance per protocol execution, serves as the building block for private set intersection (PSI) protocols (Meadows, 1986; Huberman et al., 1999). PSI lets two parties learn only the intersection of their sets without exposing non-shared elements. Section 6 applies this methodology to join the two parties’ datasets on member identifiers.

A.2. Additive Homomorphic Encryption

An additive homomorphic encryption scheme 𝖧𝖤=(𝖧𝖤.𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖧𝖤.𝖠𝖽𝖽,𝖧𝖤.𝖣𝖾𝖼)\mathsf{HE}=(\mathsf{HE.KeyGen},\mathsf{HE.Enc},\mathsf{HE.Add},\mathsf{HE.Dec}) over message space ℳ\mathcal{M}:

  • •

    (𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄)←𝖧𝖤.𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk})\leftarrow\mathsf{HE.KeyGen}(1^{\lambda})

  • •

    𝖼𝗍←𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄​(m,r)\mathsf{ct}\leftarrow\mathsf{HE.Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(m;r)

  • •

    m/⊥←𝖧𝖤.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄(𝖼𝗍)m/\bot\leftarrow\mathsf{HE.Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}(\mathsf{ct})

  • •

    Homomorphic addition: 𝖧𝖤.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄(𝖧𝖤.𝖠𝖽𝖽(𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄(m1),𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄(m2)))=(m1+m2)\mathsf{HE.Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}(\mathsf{HE.Add}(\mathsf{HE.Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(m_{1}),\mathsf{HE.Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(m_{2})))=(m_{1}+m_{2}) ∀m1,m2∈ℳ\forall m_{1},m_{2}\in\mathcal{M}.

  • •

    Homomorphic multiplication with constant: 𝖧𝖤.𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄(𝖧𝖤.𝖠𝖽𝖽(c,𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄(m)))=(c⋅m)\mathsf{HE.Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}(\mathsf{HE.Add}(c,\mathsf{HE.Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(m)))=(c\cdot m) ∀c,m∈ℳ\forall c,m\in\mathcal{M}.

We overload 𝖧𝖤.𝖠𝖽𝖽\mathsf{HE.Add} to denote both homomorphic addition and scalar multiplication. Each homomorphic evaluation is implicitly followed by a refresh operation: adding an encryption of zero so the resulting ciphertext’s randomness is independent of the originals. For Paillier encryption (Paillier, 1999), which rests on the Decisional Composite Residuosity assumption, homomorphically evaluated ciphertexts are statistically identical to fresh ones. See (Paillier, 1999) for formal correctness and CPA security definitions.

We also use traditional randomized symmetric encryption (𝖲𝗒𝗆.𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇,𝖲𝗒𝗆.𝖤𝗇𝖼,𝖲𝗒𝗆.𝖣𝖾𝖼)(\mathsf{Sym.KeyGen},\mathsf{Sym.Enc},\mathsf{Sym.Dec}).

A.3. Differential Privacy: Randomized Response Mechanism

We use the traditional local DP algorithm called randomized response (Warner, 1965). For records taking one of kk values {1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,k\}, the mechanism ℳ:{1,…,k}→{1,…,k}\mathcal{M}:\{1,\ldots,k\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,k\} retains input ii with probability eϵeϵ+k−1\frac{e^{\epsilon}}{e^{\epsilon}+k-1} and flips it to each of the other (k−1)(k-1) values with probability 1eϵ+k−1\frac{1}{e^{\epsilon}+k-1}:

𝖯𝗋[ℳ(i)=i]\displaystyle\mathsf{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(i)=i] =eϵeϵ+k−1\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\epsilon}}{e^{\epsilon}+k-1}
𝖯𝗋[ℳ(i)∈{1,⋯k}∖{i}]\displaystyle\mathsf{Pr}[\mathcal{M}(i)\in\{1,\cdots k\}\setminus\{i\}] =k−1eϵ+k−1.\displaystyle=\frac{k-1}{e^{\epsilon}+k-1}.

The privacy parameter ϵ\epsilon quantifies the tradeoff: a larger ϵ\epsilon means a higher probability that any record was not falsified.

Appendix B Additional Metric Algorithms

This appendix specifies two additional fairness metrics whose PPRE adaptations have been fully designed but are not yet deployed in production. Both follow the same three-part structure as the deployed metrics in Section 5: standard definition, probabilistic adaptation, and HE computation strategy.

B.1. POT: Pointwise Outcome Test

POT is a candidate-side metric for evaluating score-producing models. LOT evaluates ranking fairness for listing models via adjacent-rank comparisons. POT evaluates calibration fairness for scoring models: it checks whether the expected outcome at a given score level is the same across demographic groups.

Standard definition.

Given observed triplets (Si,Yi,Ri)(S_{i},Y_{i},R_{i}) (predicted score, realized outcome, and group label), POT tests whether the regression function 𝔼[Y∣S=s,R=j]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid S=s,R=j] is approximately equal across groups jj. The test uses nonparametric (Nadaraya-Watson) kernel regression at QQ reference points {s1,…,sQ}\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{Q}\} (typically score deciles):

(10) m^j​(sq)=∑i=1n𝕀⁡(Ri=j)⋅Kh​(Si−sq)⋅Yi∑i=1n𝕀⁡(Ri=j)⋅Kh​(Si−sq)\hat{m}_{j}(s_{q})=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}(R_{i}=j)\cdot K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})\cdot Y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}(R_{i}=j)\cdot K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})}

where Kh​(⋅)K_{h}(\cdot) is a Gaussian kernel with bandwidth hh. Disparities across groups are summarized by a Discounted Total Impact (DTI) metric:

(11) DTIa,b=∑q=1Qwq⋅(m^a​(sq)−m^b​(sq))\text{DTI}_{a,b}=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}w_{q}\cdot\bigl(\hat{m}_{a}(s_{q})-\hat{m}_{b}(s_{q})\bigr)

where wqw_{q} are position-dependent discount weights.

Probabilistic adaptation.

Replace the hard group indicator 𝕀⁡(Ri=j)\mathbb{I}(R_{i}=j) with the BISG posterior 𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j). This modulates each individual’s contribution to the group-specific regression by their probability of membership:

(12) m^j​(sq)=∑i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅Kh​(Si−sq)⋅Yi∑i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅Kh​(Si−sq).\hat{m}_{j}(s_{q})=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})\cdot Y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})}.

This is an instance of the model performance disparity estimator (Equation 4) with the test value modulated by the kernel weight.

HE computation strategy.

POT composes three adaptation patterns:

  1. (1)

    Pre-encryption comparison (Section 3.4). P2 holds the scores SiS_{i}, outcomes YiY_{i}, and the kernel function KhK_{h}. P2 pre-computes the kernel-weighted outcome products Kh​(Si−sq)⋅YiK_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})\cdot Y_{i} and kernel weights Kh​(Si−sq)K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q}) at each reference point sqs_{q} in plaintext, then encrypts both quantities.

  2. (2)

    Ratio estimation (Section 3.1). After the encrypted join, P1 computes per-group, per-reference-point aggregates:

    𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(Numj,q)\displaystyle\mathsf{HE.Enc}(\text{Num}_{j,q}) =⨁i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⊙𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(Kh​(Si−sq)⋅Yi)\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\odot\mathsf{HE.Enc}\!\bigl(K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})\cdot Y_{i}\bigr)
    𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(Denj,q)\displaystyle\mathsf{HE.Enc}(\text{Den}_{j,q}) =⨁i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⊙𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(Kh​(Si−sq)).\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\odot\mathsf{HE.Enc}\!\bigl(K_{h}(S_{i}-s_{q})\bigr).

    Random masking is applied before transfer to P2.

  3. (3)

    Plaintext post-processing. P2 decrypts, divides to obtain m^j​(sq)\hat{m}_{j}(s_{q}) at each reference point, computes the DTI in plaintext, and applies bootstrap significance testing (Section 3.5) to assess statistical significance.

LOT and POT share a key structural property: demographic weights come entirely from P1’s data, and outcome values come entirely from P2’s data. For LOT these outcome values are score differences; for POT they are kernel-weighted outcomes. This clean partition maps directly onto the HE computation model: P1 multiplies plaintext weights against P2’s ciphertexts and sums.

B.2. MQOS-AUC: Minimum Quality of Service-AUC

MQOS-AUC is a viewer-side metric that compares group-specific Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) against the global AUC. AUC measures the probability that a model ranks a randomly chosen positive instance above a randomly chosen negative instance. MQOS-AUC checks whether this discriminative quality differs across demographic groups.

Fairness criterion.

MQOS-AUC flags a disparity when:

(13) AUCglobal−AUC​[j]>τ,for any group ​j\text{AUC}_{\text{global}}-\text{AUC}[j]>\tau,\quad\text{for any group }j

where τ\tau is a pre-specified tolerance threshold. A violation indicates that group jj receives meaningfully worse model discrimination quality than the overall population.

PPRE implements two algorithm variants for computing probabilistic group-level AUC under HE constraints. The choice between them depends on dataset size and computational budget.

B.2.1. Algorithm 1: Probabilistic ROC-AUC

This algorithm constructs the group-specific ROC curve via a single sorted pass through the data and computes AUC using the trapezoidal rule.

Probabilistic TPR and FPR.

For group jj, the probabilistic true positive rate and false positive rate at threshold tt are:

(14) TPRj​(t)\displaystyle\text{TPR}_{j}(t) =∑i:Yi=1𝖯𝗋(Ri=j)⋅𝕀(si≥t)∑i:Yi=1𝖯𝗋(Ri=j)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i:\,Y_{i}=1}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq t)}{\sum_{i:\,Y_{i}=1}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)}
(15) FPRj​(t)\displaystyle\text{FPR}_{j}(t) =∑i:Yi=0𝖯𝗋(Ri=j)⋅𝕀(si≥t)∑i:Yi=0𝖯𝗋(Ri=j)\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i:\,Y_{i}=0}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathbb{I}(s_{i}\geq t)}{\sum_{i:\,Y_{i}=0}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)}

where sis_{i} is the model score for individual ii and YiY_{i} is the true label.

AUC via trapezoidal rule.

Using all nn distinct score values as thresholds, sorted in descending order, the probabilistic AUC for group jj is:

(16) AUC​[j]=∑m=1n12​(FPRj​(tm+1)−FPRj​(tm))⋅(TPRj​(tm)+TPRj​(tm+1)).\text{AUC}[j]=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\text{FPR}_{j}(t_{m+1})-\text{FPR}_{j}(t_{m})\bigr)\cdot\bigl(\text{TPR}_{j}(t_{m})+\text{TPR}_{j}(t_{m+1})\bigr).
HE computation strategy.

The algorithm requires sorting instances by score and incrementally computing cumulative weighted sums. Sorting requires comparison, which ciphertext space does not support. P2 holds the model scores and labels, so P2 sorts unilaterally.

  1. (1)

    Pre-encryption comparison (Section 3.4). P2 sorts all instances in descending order by score and pre-computes label-based indicators. For each instance ii in sorted order, P2 encrypts a tuple containing the label indicator and a constant 11.

  2. (2)

    Cumulative weighted aggregation. P1 processes instances in the pre-sorted order. For each group jj, P1 maintains running weighted sums of true positives and false positives using homomorphic scalar multiplication (by 𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)) and addition. At each step, the cumulative sums correspond to TPRj​(t)\text{TPR}_{j}(t) and FPRj​(t)\text{FPR}_{j}(t) at the current threshold, up to normalization.

  3. (3)

    Trapezoidal area increments. Each step’s contribution to the AUC integral (Equation 16) is a linear combination of the current and previous cumulative sums, computable in HE. The denominators (total positive and negative weights per group) are accumulated in parallel via ratio estimation (Section 3.1).

  4. (4)

    Decryption and normalization. P2 decrypts the accumulated numerator and denominator terms and computes the final AUC values in plaintext.

The computational complexity is O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) (dominated by sorting) with O⁡(k)O(k) additional memory where kk is the number of demographic groups.

B.2.2. Algorithm 2: Sampled Mann-Whitney AUC

This algorithm uses the Mann-Whitney U statistic. The statistic provides an equivalent definition of AUC: the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is scored higher than a randomly chosen negative instance.

Probabilistic Mann-Whitney AUC.

For a set SS of randomly sampled positive-negative pairs, the probabilistic group-jj AUC is:

(17) AUC​[j]=∑(i,ℓ)∈S𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅𝖯𝗋⁡(Rℓ=j)⋅𝕀⁡(si>sℓ)∑(i,ℓ)∈S𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅𝖯𝗋⁡(Rℓ=j)\text{AUC}[j]=\frac{\sum_{(i,\ell)\in S}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathsf{Pr}(R_{\ell}=j)\cdot\mathbb{I}(s_{i}>s_{\ell})}{\sum_{(i,\ell)\in S}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathsf{Pr}(R_{\ell}=j)}

where each pair (i,ℓ)∈S(i,\ell)\in S satisfies Yi=1Y_{i}=1 (positive) and Yℓ=0Y_{\ell}=0 (negative). Group membership probabilities determine each pair’s contribution to group jj’s AUC.

HE computation strategy.

The sampled Mann-Whitney algorithm requires comparison indicators and pair-weight products. Neither is directly computable in HE. The adaptation exploits the data partition:

  1. (1)

    Pre-encryption comparison (Section 3.4). P2 generates random positive-negative pairs from its data, pre-computes the comparison indicator 𝕀⁡(si>sℓ)\mathbb{I}(s_{i}>s_{\ell}) in plaintext, and encrypts the result.

  2. (2)

    Weight computation. P1 holds the race probabilities for both members of each pair. The pair weight 𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅𝖯𝗋⁡(Rℓ=j)\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathsf{Pr}(R_{\ell}=j) is a product of two plaintext values held by P1, computed entirely in plaintext.

  3. (3)

    Ratio estimation (Section 3.1). P1 computes the weighted ciphertext sum:

    𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼​(Num​[j])\displaystyle\mathsf{HE.Enc}(\text{Num}[j]) =⨁(i,ℓ)∈S[𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅𝖯𝗋⁡(Rℓ=j)]⊙𝖧𝖤.𝖤𝗇𝖼⁡(𝕀⁡(si>sℓ))\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{(i,\ell)\in S}\bigl[\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot\mathsf{Pr}(R_{\ell}=j)\bigr]\odot\mathsf{HE.Enc}\!\bigl(\mathbb{I}(s_{i}>s_{\ell})\bigr)

    with the denominator accumulated in parallel. Random masking is applied before transfer; P2 decrypts and divides.

The computational complexity is O⁡(m)O(m), where m=|S|m=|S| is the number of sampled pairs. This cost is independent of the total dataset size nn. The sampled variant is therefore preferable for very large datasets where O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) or O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) becomes expensive.

B.2.3. Algorithm Comparison

Both algorithms use the same HE adaptation strategy: P2 pre-computes all comparison and sorting operations, and P1 performs weighted linear aggregation in ciphertext space. Dataset scale and acceptable approximation error determine the choice between them.

Appendix C Additional Disparity Estimator Types

The model performance disparity estimator (Equation 4) covers the three fairness metrics deployed in production. Two additional estimator types extend the framework to other measurement tasks.

C.1. Output Metric Disparity Estimator

This estimator applies to outcome equity measurements or product equity measurements: disaggregated evaluations of a scalar outcome YY that is not derived from a model’s predictions. It computes group-wise sample means on YY directly:

(18) μ⁡[j]=∑i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)⋅Yi∑i=1n𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j),∀j∈{1,…,k}\mu[j]=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\cdot Y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)},\;\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}

This is a special case of Equation 4 with f⁡(Yi,Y^i)=Yif(Y_{i},\hat{Y}_{i})=Y_{i}. It is linear in the test values and computable under additive HE via the same ratio estimation pattern.

C.2. Probabilistic Count Disparity Estimator

This is an inclusiveness measurement: it estimates whether at least a threshold number TT of members from a race/ethnicity group are present in a member pool. For threshold T=1T=1 and group jj:

𝖯E​q​u​i​t​y\displaystyle\mathsf{P}_{Equity} =𝖯𝗋⁡(Nj≥1|Np​o​o​l)=1−𝖯𝗋⁡(Nj=0|Np​o​o​l)\displaystyle=\mathsf{Pr}(N_{j}\geq 1|N_{pool})=1-\mathsf{Pr}(N_{j}=0|N_{pool})
(19) 𝖯E​q​u​i​t​y\displaystyle\mathsf{P}_{Equity} =1−∏iNp​o​o​l(1−𝖯𝗋⁡(Ri=j)).\displaystyle=1-\prod_{i}^{N_{pool}}\Big(1-\mathsf{Pr}(R_{i}=j)\Big)\;.

The measuring party compares this to a specified probability level, e.g. 𝖯E​q​u​i​t​y≷0.90\mathsf{P}_{Equity}\gtrless 0.90, to assess with 90%90\% certainty whether the pool includes at least one member from the group of interest. When T>1T>1, Nj∼PoiBinN_{j}\sim\text{PoiBin}, requiring more detailed calculations.

This estimator is non-linear, so it cannot be computed under additive HE. However, it depends only on race/ethnicity probabilities known to P1P_{1} and pool membership from P2P_{2}, making it directly feasible under the two-party protocol without homomorphic computation.

Appendix D BISG Quality Validation

We validated BISG outputs by comparing them against Self-ID survey responses using cross-entropy. The Self-ID survey covers a self-selected subpopulation, making this an imperfect comparison, but it provides the best available ground truth.

We compared BISG variants using different input combinations:

  • •

    Baseline BISG: surname and geolocation (ZIP code) only.

  • •

    BIFSG: BISG extended with first name distributions from the Harvard Dataverse survey (Tzioumis, 2018).

  • •

    BISF: surname and first name only, without geolocation.

Figure 2 shows the results. BIFSG does not meaningfully improve over baseline BISG; the first name signal adds minimal discriminative power. BISF yields slightly lower overall cross-entropy but diminished performance for smaller groups with lower base rates. Geolocation provides critical signal for geographically concentrated groups, and removing it hurts those estimates. We therefore use baseline BISG for all production measurements.

Appendix E Sample Disparity Measurements

We present sample measurements that demonstrate end-to-end PPRE operation using the basic disparity estimators from Section 5. These measurements use the output metric and model performance estimators on illustrative tasks.

E.1. Seniority Share (Output Metric)

Using the output metric disparity estimator (Equation 18), we estimated the fraction of members holding senior roles across all six OMB race/ethnicity categories. Here YiY_{i} is a seniority indicator computed from member profile entries. Table 7 shows the results for a random sample of the U.S. member population.

The White and Black group estimates agree in relative order with a separate internal analysis (Baird and Kavanagh-Smith, 2024) that used Self-ID survey responses only (W:0.3459>B/A:0.3337W\!:\!0.3459>B/A\!:\!0.3337). The estimated magnitudes differ because the two measurements cover statistically dissimilar populations: PPRE covers the broader U.S. member population, while the comparison measurement is restricted to Self-ID respondents.

E.2. False Positive Rate (Model Performance)

Using the model performance disparity estimator (Equation 4), we computed group-wise false positive rates for a hypothetical AI classification model. Here YY is the ground truth classification and Y^\hat{Y} is the model’s predicted classification.
